newsitem.title: LATVIA: Baltic markets look forward to boost from pensions.
newsitem.headline: Baltic markets look forward to boost from pensions.

text.p: The Baltic states of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia are all moving ahead with legislation to introduce private pensions, which experts say will provide a major boost both to local markets and the economy.
The three small countries, with a combined population of eight million, all threw off Communism and launched market reforms when they quit the former Soviet Union in 1991.
Their state-run pension schemes are all having problems collecting revenues and are likely to face troubles meeting commitments in the future.
Advisors say Latvia is at the moment leading the three Baltic states in introducing legislation needed to form private pension funds.
The legislation is set for a second reading in parliament soon and includes provisions to set up a regulatory body, vital for the sound functioning of a private pension system.
"This is really important for economic growth," said Louise Fox, a World Bank senior economist who is advising the Latvian and Lithuanian authorities on pension fund legislation.

She said that around one percent of Latvia's 2.7 million population would probably take part in some form of private pension scheme in the first years of it being introduced, rising to around 20 percent after around 10 years.
"Gross domestic product (GDP) in Latvia could be as much as 10 percent higher after 10 years," Fox added.
She said that the Latvian legislation included an option partially to opt out of the state scheme, although this would not be possible in the first year of implementation.
Local stock markets and capital markets are also looking forward to a from private pensions.
All three Baltic states have stock markets which have become increasingly popular with small investors but lack the depth of funds that allow larger capital raising exercises.
Also, the local banking markets lack long-term funds, which can be lent for 10 years or more and are vital for housing loans and for capital for companies.
"This is only partly a social issue, the rest is a financial issue. It helps support a stable stock market," said Vilija Kostelnickiene, World Bank operations officer in Lithuania.
She said that Lithuanian private pension legislation was still being drawn up but it was likely that a draft would be submitted to the government this month.
Estonia is the smallest Baltic states and is considered to have the most sophisticated banking sector, but it has not made progress so far on pensions.
"They are in the very early stages," said the World Bank's Fox.
